subtitle: Step through 10 turning points from Iron Age Celtic hillforts and Claudius's AD 43 invasion to Boudicca, Vindolanda, Hadrian's Wall, and Roman Baths.

milestones.title: Celtic Tribes, Giant Hillforts & Thatched Roundhouses
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Iron Age builders leave NO chimney hole at the top of a thatched roundhouse roof?
milestones.imageCaption: A reconstructed Iron Age roundhouse at Butser Ancient Farm with woven wattle-and-daub walls and a tall cone-shaped thatched roof.
milestones.provenance: Butser Ancient Farm / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)
milestones.catalyst: Centuries before Roman soldiers arrived, Iron Age Britain was home to proud Celtic tribes such as the Iceni, Catuvellauni, and Brigantes. Families farmed wheat and barley, built giant earth hillforts like Maiden Castle, and crafted twisted gold torcs and bronze shields.
milestones.turningPoint: Celtic children helped grind grain on heavy stone querns, tended sheep and cattle, wove colourful woollen checks on upright looms, and listened to bards and Druids tell stories around the central fire.
milestones.impact: Celtic roundhouses had no chimney hole—letting gentle woodsmoke filter through the straw stopped sparks catching fire, kept beetles away, and smoked meat hanging from the rafters!
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (55–54 BC): Julius Caesar's Two Expeditions Across the Channel.

ks2.story: Centuries before Roman soldiers arrived, Iron Age Britain was home to proud Celtic tribes such as the Iceni, Catuvellauni, and Brigantes. Families farmed wheat and barley, built giant earth hillforts like Maiden Castle, and crafted twisted gold torcs and bronze shields.

ks2.childrenLife: Celtic children helped grind grain on heavy stone querns, tended sheep and cattle, wove colourful woollen checks on upright looms, and listened to bards and Druids tell stories around the central fire.
ks2.quote: “The island is thickly populated with homesteads and vast numbers of cattle, and they use gold coins or iron bars for money.” — Julius Caesar, Gallic War V.12 (tr. Edwards 1917)
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Why did Iron Age builders leave NO chimney hole at the top of a thatched roundhouse roof?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: A chimney hole would pull up a rush of air and send fiery sparks into the dry straw roof! Letting smoke seep slowly through the thatch prevented fires and smoked meat.

milestones.title: Julius Caesar's Two Expeditions Across the Channel
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Did Julius Caesar conquer Britain permanently in 55–54 BC?
milestones.imageCaption: An Iron Age British gold stater coin minted around 55–45 BC—showing prosperous trade across the Channel at the time of Julius Caesar.
milestones.provenance: Portable Antiquities Scheme / West Yorkshire Archaeology Service (CC BY-SA 4.0)
milestones.catalyst: Famous Roman general Julius Caesar sailed from Gaul to Kent in 55 BC and returned in 54 BC with 800 ships. Although Roman legionaries won battles and demanded tribute, Channel storms battered Caesar’s fleet and trouble in Gaul forced him to sail back.
milestones.turningPoint: Children on the Kent cliffs watched hundreds of wooden Roman warships row ashore while fast two-horse Celtic chariots raced along the pebble beaches.
milestones.impact: Caesar did NOT conquer Britain permanently—no Roman forts stayed behind, and British tribes ruled themselves for nearly a hundred more years, though trade with Rome grew rapidly.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (AD 43): Emperor Claudius Invades with 40,000 Troops & War Elephants.

ks2.quote: “The Britons leap down from their chariots and fight on foot with extraordinary speed and steadiness.” — Julius Caesar, Gallic War IV.33
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Did Julius Caesar conquer Britain permanently in 55–54 BC?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: No! Caesar returned to Gaul both times without leaving soldiers behind; Britain stayed independent for another 97 years until AD 43.

milestones.title: Emperor Claudius Invades with 40,000 Troops & War Elephants
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How many soldiers landed in Emperor Claudius’s AD 43 invasion force, and which Kentish port became their main gateway?
milestones.imageCaption: Roman legionaries locking curved rectangular scutum shields into the armoured testudo ("tortoise") formation.
milestones.catalyst: Wanting Britain’s silver, tin, lead, and grain—and eager to prove himself a mighty conqueror—Emperor Claudius sent General Aulus Plautius across the Channel with 40,000 professional soldiers. They landed at Richborough in Kent and defeated Caratacus at the River Medway.
milestones.turningPoint: Imagine being a British child in Colchester watching giant grey war elephants and thousands of soldiers in gleaming iron strip armour march past thatched roundhouses for the very first time!
milestones.impact: Claudius travelled from Rome with war elephants to lead the triumphant march into Camulodunum (Colchester), turning southern Britain into Rome’s newest province: Britannia.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (AD 60–61): Queen Boudicca's Great Rebellion & Burning of Londinium.

ks2.quote: “Claudius crossed over to Britain, joined his legions waiting by the Thames, captured Camulodunum, and won over numerous tribes.” — Cassius Dio, Roman History 60.21 (PD tr. 1925)
ks2.detectiveQuestion: How many soldiers landed in Emperor Claudius’s AD 43 invasion force, and which Kentish port became their main gateway?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Around 40,000 soldiers (20,000 citizen legionaries and 20,000 auxiliaries), landing at Richborough in Kent.

milestones.title: Queen Boudicca's Great Rebellion & Burning of Londinium
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Which three Roman towns were burned to red ash during Boudicca’s rebellion?
milestones.imageCaption: Bronze monument by Thomas Thornycroft at Westminster Bridge showing Iceni Queen Boudicca and her two daughters in a war chariot.
milestones.catalyst: When Iceni King Prasutagus died in AD 60, Roman officials broke his peaceful will, seized Iceni farms, and flogged Queen Boudicca. Rising up with the Trinovantes while Governor Suetonius was in Wales, Boudicca burned Camulodunum, Londinium, and Verulamium to the ground.
milestones.turningPoint: Families in bustling timber-built Londinium had to pack whatever they could carry and flee south across the Thames before fire swept through every shop and home.
milestones.impact: Archaeologists digging beneath London still uncover a 30cm layer of bright red burnt clay and melted glass from AD 60! Yet at the Battle of Watling Street (AD 61), 10,000 disciplined legionaries defeated Boudicca in a narrow wooded valley.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. AD 100): Postcards in the Mud: Wooden Letters at Vindolanda Fort.

milestones.title: Postcards in the Mud: Wooden Letters at Vindolanda Fort
milestones.enquiryQuestion: What clever natural condition stopped the thin wooden Vindolanda letters from rotting away for nearly 2,000 years?
milestones.imageCaption: Vindolanda Tablet 291: Claudia Severa’s ink birthday party invitation written on wafer-thin wood around AD 100.
milestones.catalyst: At Vindolanda Fort in Northumberland, wet oxygen-free mud preserved hundreds of thin wooden ink letters like time capsules. They include Claudia Severa inviting her friend Sulpicia Lepidina to her birthday party on 11 September, and a parcel list sending warm woollen socks and underpants!
milestones.turningPoint: Archaeologists also found tiny Roman children’s leather shoes in the Vindolanda mud—proving commanders’ children played and grew up right inside chilly northern frontier forts!
milestones.impact: Claudia Severa’s greeting at the bottom of Tablet 291 is the oldest surviving example of Latin handwriting by a woman anywhere in the world.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (AD 122): Hadrian's Wall: 73 Miles of Stone & Troops From Three Continents.

ks2.childrenLife: Archaeologists also found tiny Roman children’s leather shoes in the Vindolanda mud—proving commanders’ children played and grew up right inside chilly northern frontier forts!

ks2.detectiveQuestion: What clever natural condition stopped the thin wooden Vindolanda letters from rotting away for nearly 2,000 years?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Deep, wet, oxygen-free mud sealed out air and bacteria that normally rot wood!

milestones.title: Hadrian's Wall: 73 Miles of Stone & Troops From Three Continents
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How long was Hadrian’s Wall in modern miles, and what stood at every Roman mile to control travellers and taxes?
milestones.imageCaption: Milecastle 39 ('Castle Nick') and Hadrian's Wall climbing the steep crags near Steel Rigg in Northumberland.
milestones.catalyst: Emperor Hadrian visited Britain in AD 122 and ordered soldiers to build a stone wall 73 miles (80 Roman miles) from Wallsend on the Tyne to Bowness-on-Solway, complete with guarded Milecastle gates every mile and 16 forts like Housesteads.
milestones.turningPoint: Children growing up in fort towns (vici) outside the Wall heard soldiers speaking Latin alongside accents and languages from Gaul, Syria, Spain, and North Africa!
milestones.impact: Auxiliary soldiers and traders stationed along the frontier came from across Europe, Syria, and North Africa—including the Unit of Aurelian Moors at Burgh-by-Sands, Syrian trader Barates and his British wife Regina, and North African freedman Victor at Arbeia.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (AD 70–200): Straight Stone Roads, Forums & Aquae Sulis Steam Baths.

ks2.quote: “Hadrian was the first to build a wall eighty miles long to separate the Romans from the barbarians.” — Historia Augusta, Life of Hadrian 11.2

milestones.title: Straight Stone Roads, Forums & Aquae Sulis Steam Baths
milestones.enquiryQuestion: What curved bronze tool did Roman bathers use with olive oil instead of soap to scrape away dirt and sweat?
milestones.imageCaption: The lead-lined Great Bath at Aquae Sulis (Bath, Somerset), fed by natural steaming hot mineral springs.
milestones.catalyst: Roman engineers laid 10,000 miles of cambered stone highways linking bustling walled towns with central forums, amphitheatres like Caerleon, aqueducts, sewers, and public bathhouses like Aquae Sulis (Bath), where bathers scraped off scented olive oil using a curved bronze strigil.
milestones.turningPoint: Town children practised scratching Latin letters onto wax tablets with a metal stylus, snacked on imported figs, cherries, and walnuts in the forum, and watched noisy gladiator displays.
milestones.impact: Cambered stone roads sloped gently to side ditches so rainwater drained away, allowing armies, carts, and imperial post riders to travel fast in every season.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (AD 160–350): Hypocaust Villa Mosaics vs. Countryside Roundhouses.

milestones.title: Hypocaust Villa Mosaics vs. Countryside Roundhouses
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Roughly how many out of every ten people in Roman Britain still lived and farmed in the countryside rather than in stone towns or villas?
milestones.imageCaption: The famous Cupid riding a Dolphin floor mosaic at Fishbourne Roman Palace in West Sussex, crafted from thousands of tiny stone tesserae.
milestones.catalyst: Wealthy Romano-British leaders built grand country villas like Fishbourne and Chedworth, warmed underneath by hypocaust furnaces pushing hot air between stacks of brick tiles (pilae) below colourful mosaic floors. Yet nearly nine out of ten Britons still farmed in rural roundhouses!
milestones.turningPoint: While a rich villa child walked bare-footed across warm dolphin mosaics, a countryside farm child still slept under thatch and drove cattle to market along the new Roman road.
milestones.impact: Comparing rich villas with rural farmsteads shows historians that Roman rule brought luxury to wealthy elites while everyday farming life continued much as before for most countryside families.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (AD 410): Emperor Honorius's Reply & Buried Silver Treasure Hoards.

ks2.childrenLife: While a rich villa child walked bare-footed across warm dolphin mosaics, a countryside farm child still slept under thatch and drove cattle to market along the new Roman road.
ks2.quote: Each large mosaic floor required hundreds of thousands of hand-cut limestone, chalk, and red tile cubes called tesserae.
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Roughly how many out of every ten people in Roman Britain still lived and farmed in the countryside rather than in stone towns or villas?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Around nine out of ten people (85–90%) lived in the countryside!

milestones.title: Emperor Honorius's Reply & Buried Silver Treasure Hoards
milestones.enquiryQuestion: In what famous year did Emperor Honorius tell the towns of Roman Britain that they must look to their own defences?
milestones.imageCaption: The gilded silver "Empress" pepper pot from the Hoxne Hoard, buried for safekeeping in Suffolk shortly after AD 407.
milestones.provenance: Photographed by BabelStone / Wikimedia Commons (CC0 1.0 Public Domain)
milestones.catalyst: Attacked by Picts from Scotland, Scotti from Ireland, and Saxon raiders across the North Sea while enemy armies threatened Italy itself, Rome pulled its legions out of Britain. In AD 410 Emperor Honorius told British towns to defend themselves, and anxious families buried silver treasures like the Hoxne and Mildenhall hoards.
milestones.turningPoint: Families carefully packed silver spoons, coins, and spice pots into oak chests and buried them in fields hoping to return—leaving hidden treasure for metal detectorists 1,500 years later!
milestones.impact: Without soldiers’ pay, Roman coin minting ceased and town bathhouses slowly crumbled—opening a new chapter as Anglo-Saxon kingdoms grew across eastern and southern Britain.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (Today): Rome's Living Legacy: Cities, Roads, Words & Our Calendar.

milestones.title: Rome's Living Legacy: Cities, Roads, Words & Our Calendar
milestones.enquiryQuestion: What Latin word for a Roman camp or fort gives us modern city names like Chester, Manchester, Colchester, and Lancaster?
milestones.imageCaption: The Roman Multangular Tower at Eboracum (York), standing strong for over 1,700 years since c. AD 306.
milestones.catalyst: Even after the legions left, 367 years of Roman rule shaped Britain forever: Londinium grew into London, "-chester" and "-caster" cities mark Roman forts (castra), modern highways follow straight Roman roads, and we still use the Latin ABC alphabet, Roman numerals, and the 12-month calendar!
milestones.turningPoint: Every time you write the alphabet at school, read clock numerals (I–XII), celebrate a birthday in July or August, or travel to Manchester or Chester, you are using a Roman legacy!
milestones.impact: From July (Julius Caesar) and August (Emperor Augustus) to Christianity, written laws, sweet apples, cabbages, rabbits, and stinging nettles, Roman clues surround us every single day.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Completes all 10 turning points in The Romans in Britain (450 BC–AD 410).
